native_result.query: At what Socioeconomic levels is the advantage in completion rates for Black students more pronounced?
native_result.HypoA: The advantage in BA degree completion rates for Black students becomes more pronounced at higher SES levels indicated by a positive interaction term SES*is_Black(coefficient:0.6271 (significant))
native_result.HypoB: The relative advantage in bachelor's (BA) degree completion for Black students is most pronounced at the HIGHEST socioeconomic levels, where the completion-rate gap relative to White students narrows to a minimum and essentially disappears, whereas it is wide and significant at lower SES levels. Within the top SES quartile Black students reach 3.03% vs 3.67% for White (−0.64 pp, rate ratio 0.83, Fisher p=0.72, statistically indistinguishable), versus Q1 (−1.34 pp, 0.25, p=0.017), Q2 (−2.99 pp, 0.31, p=0.0003) and Q3 (−2.10 pp, 0.44, p=0.025). A continuous logistic model (BA ~ SES×race) shows the BA-SES gradient is significantly steeper for Black students (SES_z slope 0.726 vs 0.161 for White; interaction p=0.003); the log-odds gap narrows from ~1.81 (low SES) to ~0.12 (high SES) and the predicted Black/White ratio climbs from 0.17 to 0.89. Robustness via tertiles (0.14→0.58) and Black-vs-rest (0.33→0.82) reproduces the monotonic pattern. Caveat: relative advantage only; absolute Black>White advantage never materializes.
native_result.WorkflowB: Loaded nls_ses_processed.csv (8,773×8, no missing). Computed per-race and per-SES BA completion rates; binned SES into full-sample quartiles (primary) and tertiles (robustness). Per SES level: 2x2 Black-vs-White/rest tables with pp difference, rate ratio and Fisher exact test. Continuous logistic regression BA ~ SES_z * RACE for the SES-gradient comparison and narrowing log-odds gap. Evidence saved to analysis/evidence_summary.txt.
